title: Putting Africa’s Capital to Work
gist: BCG argues Africa's $0.9 trillion of pension and insurance assets, under 2% allocated to alternatives versus 20-25% in North America, could replace shrinking DFI and foreign private-capital funding. Barriers are trustee capability, mismatched fund domiciles and high local sovereign yields, and BCG proposes five coordinated reforms within 24 months.

themes.theme: Africa's private capital gap and donor dependence

insights.claim: Only about $5 billion of private capital was deployed in Africa in 2025, against an unmet SME financing need of about $330 billion and an annual infrastructure financing gap of roughly $100 billion.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Shows the size of the unserved opportunity for any capital that can reach African private markets.
insights.locator: Africa's Institutions: A Vast Untapped Resource

insights.claim: DFIs and foreign investors supplied more than 75% of African private capital LP commitments in 2022-2025, with DFIs alone at 51%, foreign commercial LPs at about 32% and local African investors only 17%.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: African PE fundraising is structurally dependent on external, policy-sensitive money.
insights.locator: Africa's Institutions: A Vast Untapped Resource

insights.claim: DFI fundraising for African private capital grew 17% a year in 2022-2025 despite global headwinds, but is expected to be challenged because the US, UK, France and Germany are cutting ODA, with Sub-Saharan Africa facing a 16-28% ODA decline between 2025 and 2027.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Donor budget cuts are a forward risk to the main funding source of African PE funds; watch fund closes and GP fundraising timelines.
insights.locator: Africa's Institutions: A Vast Untapped Resource

themes.theme: Domestic institutional capital as the substitute

insights.claim: Africa held about $4 trillion of domestic capital in 2025, of which roughly $0.9 trillion sat in pension funds and insurers, pools whose duration and local-currency profile suit alternative strategies.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A large local balance sheet exists that could replace shrinking foreign capital.
insights.locator: Africa's Institutions: A Vast Untapped Resource

insights.claim: African institutional assets compounded at 8% a year in 2018-2025, with pensions rising from about $330 billion to $550 billion and insurance from about $200 billion to $360 billion.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Steady asset growth creates a rising pool needing yield and diversification.
insights.locator: Africa's Institutions: A Vast Untapped Resource

insights.claim: Institutional asset growth was fastest outside South Africa, compounding at 25% a year in Ghana, 18% in Egypt, 17% in Nigeria and 13% in Kenya.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Frontier and second-tier markets are where institutional AUM growth, and thus future LP supply, is concentrated.
insights.locator: Africa's Institutions: A Vast Untapped Resource

insights.claim: Redirecting just 1% of regional institutional AUM into alternatives would be a one-off stock shift but would still equal more than 3.5 times current annual African private capital fundraising.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Small allocation changes by local institutions would dwarf the current fundraising base.

insights.claim: African pension and insurance portfolios are dominated by government securities, sometimes above 50%, with under 2% in alternatives versus roughly 20-25% of AUM for North American pension funds.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The allocation gap versus developed markets defines the potential re-rating of African alternatives demand.

insights.claim: Formal regulatory ceilings on alternatives far exceed actual allocations: South Africa 0.8% PE vs 15% ceiling, Nigeria 1.7% vs 10%, Kenya 0.7% vs 10%, Ghana 1.1% vs 25%.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Rules are not the binding constraint; the shortfall lies in behavior and market structure.

insights.claim: Allocation patterns differ by region, with South Africa the most diversified yet still at about 2% alternatives, Kenya below 1%, Ghana concentrated in sovereign debt, and Morocco shifting toward equities and alternatives while Egypt stays in government securities.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Morocco and Nigeria look like earlier movers; Ghana, Egypt and Kenya are the most sovereign-concentrated.

themes.theme: Why trustees rationally stay in sovereign debt

insights.claim: Local-currency sovereign yields of 15-20%+ in Egypt, Ghana and Nigeria and 10-18% in Kenya and South Africa often offer both higher returns and lower risk than African alternative managers have delivered, making conservative allocation rational.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: High risk-free local rates crowd out private assets; falling yields would be the trigger for reallocation.

insights.claim: Funds with proven track records tend to be domiciled offshore in hard currency, which clashes with local regulation and adds FX risk for local institutions, while locally accessible funds are mostly first-time, single-country, local-currency vehicles with thin track records.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A supply mismatch: good managers are inaccessible and accessible managers are unproven.

insights.claim: Pension trustees are often non-professionals who are personally accountable, prioritize capital preservation, and face asymmetric reputational risk if an alternative allocation underperforms.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Governance incentives, not capital shortage, hold back allocation; education and benchmarks matter more than pitch decks.

insights.claim: Trustees are uncomfortable with NAV-based valuations, GP fair-value marks, capital-call and exit-timing modelling against liabilities, and quarterly reporting with limited comparability, and many appointed local managers lack dedicated alternatives teams.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Opaque valuation and weak benchmarking suppress demand; transparency data providers could be an enabling niche.

insights.claim: Regulation often restricts institutions from investing in offshore vehicles such as pan-African funds domiciled in Mauritius or Luxembourg, and makes structuring and expatriating capital from locally domiciled vehicles costly.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Regulatory reform on domiciliation and offshore access is the key catalyst to watch.

insights.claim: BCG proposes five coordinated unlocks across three layers: transparent performance data and a trustee training curriculum, targeted tax, licensing and exchange-control packages for local domiciliation plus permission to invest in offshore African funds, and a consolidated pan-African syndication platform for co-investments.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Gives a checklist of milestones whose progress would signal real mobilization of local capital.
insights.locator: Five Priority Actions Can Break Down the Barriers

insights.claim: Mobilizing African institutional capital is fundamentally an ecosystem problem requiring regulators, DFIs, managers, institutions and industry bodies to act in parallel, and manager performance and liquidity must also improve through disciplined entry valuations, value creation and exit planning.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Progress will be slow and dependent on coordination; manager track records remain the gating item.

insights.claim: The window is open now because sovereign yields are decreasing, regulators are moving progressively, pension and insurance assets are growing and institutions seek diversification, and coordinated action over the next 24 months could change allocation trends.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Falling local yields reduce the opportunity cost of private assets, favoring African PE fundraising from local LPs over a two-year horizon.
insights.quote: The window of opportunity is open now
